source_text:
Οὐκ ἐδιδάξαμέν σε ῥητῶς ἀπὸ μὲν τοῦ
μύρμηκος τὸ ἄοκνον, ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς μελίσσης τὸ φιλότεχνον; Ἔστι γὰρ, ἔστιν, ὡς ἔφθην
εἰπὼν, ἀπανθήσασθαί τινα καὶ τῶν ἀλόγων πλεονεκτήματα ἁρμόζοντα λογικῇ
καταστάσει· πλήν γε ταῦτα πρὸς ἡμετέραν λέγονται αἰσχύνην καὶ ὄνειδος. Ἐπειδὴ
γὰρ Θεὸν οὐκ ἐμιμήσω, μίμησαι, φησὶ, τὸν μύρμηκα. Οὐκ εἶδές ποτε πατέρα γνήσιον
ἐπιτιμῶντα τὰ τέκνα, καὶ μετὰ πολλὴν παιδείαν εἰς μίμησιν αὐτὰ οἰκετῶν ἀνάγοντα,
καὶ ταῦτα προφανῶς λέγοντα· Μίμησαι κἂν τὸν οἰκέτην, ὑποδεέστερον μὲν τῇ ἀξίᾳ,
ὑπερέχοντα δὲ τῇ ἐπιστήμῃ; Ὅθεν ὁ 56.520 φιλάνθρωπος Θεὸς εἰς ἔνδειξιν τῆς
ἡμετέρας ἀγνωμοσύνης προσφέρει τὸν μύρμηκα ἐλέγχοντα ἡμῶν τὸν ὄκνον, καὶ τὴν
μέλιτταν ἐλέγχουσαν ἡμῶν τὴν ῥᾳθυμίαν. Καὶ δῆλον ἐκ τούτων, ὅτι οὐδὲν κακὸν
ἐγένετο παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἀλλ' ἔδωκέ σοι αἴσθησιν καὶ νοῦν διακριτικὸν, φεύγειν μὲν
τῶν ἀλόγων τὰ ἤθη, ἁρπάζειν δὲ αὐτῶν τὰ πλεονεκτήματα. ∆ύναται γὰρ καὶ ὁ λέων
εἰκὼν εἶναι ἀρετῆς, ὅταν μὴ εἰς τυραννίδα τὴν εἰκόνα, ἀλλ' εἰς ἀνδρείαν ἐκλάβῃς·
ἄλλο γάρ ἐστι τυραννὶς, καὶ ἕτερον ἀνδρεία. ∆ιὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἡ Γραφὴ τὸν ἐκ τοῦ Ἰούδα
μέλλοντα ἀνατέλλειν εὐαγγελιζομένη Σωτῆρα, φησί· Σκύμνος λέοντος Ἰούδα· ἐκ
βλαστοῦ, υἱέ μου, ἀνέβης· ἀναπεσὼν ἐκοιμήθης ὡς λέων, καὶ ὡς σκύμνος. Ὅρα
πηλίκην ὁ θεῖος λόγος ὁμοιότητα κατασκευάζει ἐκ τῶν τοῖς ἀλόγοις προσόντων
πλεονεκτημάτων. Ἔστι τοίνυν μιμεῖσθαι λέοντα μετὰ συνέσεως· ἔστι δὲ μιμεῖσθαι
καὶ ὄφιν, οὐκ ἐν τῷ ἰοβολεῖν, ἀλλ' ἐν τῷ σύνεσιν ἀναλαμβάνειν· καθὼς καὶ ὁ Σωτὴρ
τοῖς ἀποστόλοις φησί· Γίνεσθε φρόνιμοι, ὡς ὁ ὄφις. Ὅθεν, εἰ φαῦλον ἦν τὸ κτίσμα,
οὐκ ἂν εἰς μίμησιν τοῦ φαύλου προσεκαλεῖτο τὴν ἑαυτοῦ εἰκόνα, Γίνεσθε, λέγων,
φρόνιμοι ὡς ὄφις· μίμησαι τοῦ ὄφεως μὴ τὸν ἰὸν, μὴ τὸν θυμὸν, ἀλλὰ τὴν σύνεσιν.
Ἐὰν γὰρ τὸν ἰὸν μιμήσῃ, καταβοᾷ σου ∆αυῒδ κατηγορῶν καὶ λέγων· Θυμὸς αὐτοῖς
κατὰ τὴν ὁμοίωσιν τοῦ ὄφεως· ἐὰν δὲ τὴν σύνεσιν αὐτοῦ μιμήσῃ, μαθητὴς γίνῃ
Χριστοῦ τοῦ εἰπόντος· Γίνεσθε φρόνιμοι ὡς ὁ ὄφις. Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ὁ ὄφις φρονιμώτερός
ἐστι πάντων τῶν θηρίων, ὡς ἀρτίως ὑπανεγνώσθη, ἀντέθηκε τῇ φρονήσει φρόνησιν,
οὐχ ἵνα μάθῃς δόλον ποιεῖν, ἀλλ' ἵνα μάθῃς δόλον ἐκκλίνειν. βʹ. Βούλεται γὰρ ἡμᾶς
ὁ φιλάνθρωπος Θεὸς οὐχὶ κακούργους εἶναι, ἀλλὰ πανούργους· ἕτερον δέ ἐστι τὸ
πανοῦργον, καὶ ἕτερον τὸ κακοῦργον. Πανοῦργος τοίνυν ἐστὶν οὐκ εἰς τὸ μελετᾷν
κακίαν, ἀλλ' εἰς τὸ φεύγειν κακίαν· καὶ κέχρηται τῇ πανουργίᾳ οὐκ εἰς τὸ
μηχανοῤῥαφεῖν καθ' ἑτέρων, ἀλλ' εἰς τὸ τὰ ὑφ' ἑτέρων πλεκόμενα διαφεύγειν·
κακοῦργος δέ ἐστιν ὁ φονεὺς, ὁ δόλιος, ὁ ἑτέροις κακὰ τεκταινόμενος. Τοιοῦτος
φρόνιμος ὁ Ἰακὼβ, φρόνιμος ὡς ὁ ὄφις, οὐκ ἰοβόλος ὡς ὁ ὄφις.
thought_title: Imitating the useful qualities of irrational animals
orientation: The homilist continues his argument that God made nothing evil by nature, showing that Scripture itself commands imitation of the ant, bee, lion, and serpent for their useful qualities.
pass_a_gloss: Did we not teach you explicitly from the ant the unhesitating eagerness, and from the bee the craftsmanship? For it is possible, it is possible, as I was quick to say, to pluck certain excellent qualities even of the irrational animals that suit a rational condition; yet these things are said for our shame and reproach. For since you did not imitate God, imitate, he says, the ant. Have you never seen a true father rebuking his children, and after much discipline leading them to imitation of household servants, and saying these things openly: Imitate at least the household servant, inferior in rank, but surpassing in skill? Therefore the man-loving God, for a demonstration of our ingratitude, brings forward the ant convicting our sloth, and the bee convicting our negligence. And it is clear from these things, that nothing evil was made by God, but he gave you perception and a discerning mind, to flee the habits of the irrational animals, and to seize their excellent qualities. For the lion also can be an image of virtue, when you take the image not for tyranny, but for courage; for tyranny is one thing, and courage is another. Therefore also the Scripture, announcing the good news of the Savior who is about to rise from Judah, says: A lion's whelp is Judah; from a shoot, my son, you went up; reclining you slept as a lion, and as a whelp. See how great a likeness the divine word constructs from the excellent qualities that belong to the irrational animals. It is possible then to imitate a lion with understanding; and it is possible also to imitate a serpent, not in the injecting of venom, but in the taking up of understanding; just as also the Savior says to the apostles: Become prudent as the serpent. Therefore, if the creature were worthless, he would not have called his own image to imitation of the worthless thing, saying: Become prudent as the serpent; imitate of the serpent not the venom, not the anger, but the understanding. For if you imitate the venom, David cries out against you accusing and saying: Their anger is according to the likeness of the serpent; but if you imitate its understanding, you become a disciple of Christ who said: Become prudent as the serpent. For since the serpent is more prudent than all the wild beasts, as was just now read, he set prudence against prudence, not so that you may learn to devise deceit, but so that you may learn to avoid deceit. 2. For the man-loving God wishes us to be not evildoers, but prudent persons; and the prudent thing is one thing, and the evildoing thing is another. A prudent person then is one not for the meditating of evil, but for the fleeing of evil; and he uses prudence not for the weaving of plots against others, but for the escaping of the plots woven by others; and an evildoer is the murderer, the deceitful one, the one devising evils for others. Such a prudent man was Jacob, prudent as the serpent, not venom-injecting as the serpent.

choices.why: The noun form of the adjective describes the ant's quality of not hesitating or shrinking from labor; 'eagerness' captures the positive active sense rather than a mere absence of hesitation.
The compound means love of art or skill; as a quality to imitate, 'craftsmanship' conveys the bee's skilled work rather than a mere fondness for craft.
The verb means to gather or cull flowers; 'pluck' preserves the floral metaphor of selecting excellent qualities from the animals.
In this context the word denotes failure to recognize God's goodness, i.e., ingratitude toward the Creator, which fits the argument that humans slander God's creation.
The glossary requires 'prudence' for πανουργία; the adjective form is rendered as 'prudent persons' to distinguish it from the negative 'evildoers' (κακούργους).
The compound literally means to stitch or weave schemes; 'weaving of plots' preserves the metaphor of contriving against others.

Quoted as the Savior's words to the apostles; the homilist omits the second half about doves.

bible_refs.note: Quoted from the Septuagint Psalm 57:5, which corresponds to Psalm 58:4 in modern numbering.

pass_b_english: Have we not taught you explicitly to take unhesitating eagerness from the ant, and craftsmanship from the bee? For it is possible, as I said before, to pluck certain excellent qualities even from the irrational animals that suit a rational condition—yet these things are said for our shame and reproach. Since you did not imitate God, Scripture says, imitate the ant. Have you never seen a true father rebuking his children, and after much instruction leading them to imitate the household servants, saying openly: “Imitate even the servant, who is lower in rank but superior in skill”? So the God who loves humanity, to expose our ingratitude, brings forward the ant to convict our hesitation, and the bee to convict our laziness. And it is clear from these things that nothing evil was made by God; rather, he gave you perception and a discerning mind, to flee the habits of the irrational animals and to seize their excellent qualities. For the lion can also be an image of virtue, when you take the image not as tyranny but as courage—for tyranny is one thing, and courage another. Therefore Scripture, announcing the Savior who was to rise from Judah, says: “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the shoot, my son, you went up; crouching down, you slept like a lion, and like a cub” (Genesis 49:9). See how great a likeness the divine word constructs from the excellent qualities found in the irrational animals. It is possible, then, to imitate the lion with understanding; and it is possible also to imitate the serpent, not in injecting venom, but in taking on understanding—just as the Savior says to the apostles: “Be prudent as the serpent” (Matthew 10:16). Therefore, if the creature were worthless, he would not call his own image to imitate what is worthless, saying, “Be prudent as the serpent.” Imitate not the serpent’s venom, not its rage, but its understanding. For if you imitate its venom, David cries out against you in accusation, saying: “Their rage is like the likeness of the serpent” (Psalm 58:4). But if you imitate its understanding, you become a disciple of Christ, the one who said: “Be prudent as the serpent” (Matthew 10:16). For since the serpent is more prudent than all the wild beasts, as was just read, he set prudence against prudence—not so that you may learn to devise deceit, but so that you may learn to avoid deceit. For the God who loves humanity wants us to be not evildoers but prudent persons; and the prudent person is one thing, the evildoer another. The prudent person, then, is prudent not for practicing evil but for fleeing evil; he uses prudence not for weaving plots against others, but for escaping the plots woven by others. The evildoer, however, is the murderer, the deceiver, the one who contrives evils for others. Such a prudent man was Jacob—prudent as the serpent, not venomous as the serpent.

last_rejected.quote: Their rage is like the likeness of the serpent
last_rejected.source_quote: Θυμὸς αὐτοῖς κατὰ τὴν ὁμοίωσιν τοῦ ὄφεως
last_rejected.why: Source means 'their rage is according to the likeness of the serpent'; 'like the likeness' is awkward and slightly distorts meaning.
last_rejected.fix: Their rage is according to the likeness of the serpent
last_rejected.ruling: 'Like the likeness' is awkward but within normal range; 'κατὰ τὴν ὁμοίωσιν' can bear this rendering, meaning unchanged.

last_rejected.why: φησὶ refers to God speaking (implied by context of father/children analogy), not Scripture as marked speaker.
last_rejected.ruling: φησὶ is indefinite 'he says'; context (μίμησαι τὸν μύρμηκα) echoes Prov 6:6, so 'Scripture says' is reasonable.

last_rejected.why: ὄκνος means 'sloth,' 'reluctance to work,' 'hesitation' loses the specific vice of laziness; but 'hesitation' is weak. Actually within range? No, ὄκνος is specifically 'sloth/reluctance,' better 'sloth' or 'idleness.'
last_rejected.ruling: ὄκνος includes 'hesitation, reluctance, shirking'; 'hesitation' is within normal range, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.why: Subject is Christ/the Savior (ὁ Σωτήρ from prior clause), but 'he' is ambiguous; could refer to God. Context shows Christ spoke the command, so Christ set prudence against prudence.
last_rejected.ruling: Subject ambiguity of 'he' is minor; prior clause subject is ὁ ὄφις (serpent), not Christ; no real misreading.
